title: Northern Lights May Be Visible Across Parts of the U.S. as Geomagnetic Storm Hits
excerpt: A weak geomagnetic storm could bring a chance of seeing the northern lights across parts of the northern U.S. this week.
content:
Siddharth Munjal

Wed, November 18, 2026 at 8:11 PM UTC

NOAA expects heightened geomagnetic activity that could allow sightings of the northern lights in parts of the northern United States late on Nov. 17 and early on Nov. 18.

The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) expects the planetary Kp index to reach 4.67 between the three-hour intervals of 21:00 UTC on 17 November and 03:00 UTC on 18 November. The forecast is a mix of a coronal hole high-speed stream and a possible glancing blow from a coronal mass ejection (CME).

A G1 geomagnetic storm watch is in effect for both days. While G1 is the lowest classification on the NOAA geomagnetic storm scale, it can still produce auroras in parts of the northern U.S., including possibly northern Michigan and Maine.

Which Cities Have a Chance to See the Northern Lights?

Skywatchers in parts of Minnesota and Michigan have a slim chance of seeing the aurora during the storm. Forecasts have the chances at about 4% in International Falls, Minn, and around 2% in both Duluth, Minn, and Marquette, Mich. But those odds are low, meaning the northern lights are nowhere near guaranteed.

Alaska should offer better viewing opportunities, particularly near Fairbanks, where aurora activity is generally more favorable. If you want to see the lights, get away from city lights, look to the northern horizon, and check the local cloud cover before you go.

The predicted activity is associated with a high-speed stream of solar wind from a coronal hole, a region on the Sun where magnetic fields allow solar material to escape more easily.

NOAA is also tracking a CME that erupted from the Sun on Nov. 14, but forecasters have low confidence that it will have a major impact on Earth.

On November 14 at 21:27 UTC, a solar eruption was observed, which was associated with a Type II radio emission. It was associated with an estimated speed of 1,972 km per second.

G1 events are not expected to have significant impacts, but can cause minor disruptions to satellite operations, and small fluctuations in power grids. Geomagnetic activity is forecast to slowly decrease to unsettled levels on Nov. 19, according to NOAA forecasters.
